name: Aglianico del Vulture Superiore

climate.koppen_name: Temperate, no dry season, hot summer

climate: Seasons this warm ripen Sangiovese, Sémillon, Cabernet Franc, Tempranillo and Dolcetto fully without cooking off their freshness.
Sangiovese sits in its sweet spot, so the wines can show the style it is known for.

soil.rock: Shale and mudstone are fine-grained rocks that hold heat well and are moderately fertile. Limestone makes alkaline soil that drains well yet can hold water for the vines. It is usually planted to grapes valued for their acidity.
soil.top: The topsoil stores water through dry spells, but stays wet and cold after rain, which slows ripening and can swell the grapes. Its high pH can starve vines of iron and yellow the leaves, so growers plant lime-tolerant rootstocks.

land: The high ground runs about 5°F cooler than the low ground. Higher vineyards ripen later and keep more acidity, so one grape can make lighter or richer wine here depending on height.
Gentle slopes. Enough tilt to drain cold air and rain away, which lowers frost risk, yet still easy to farm by machine.

winkler: Good for generous crops of standard to good wine.

sheet.place: Aglianico del Vulture Superiore is 100% Aglianico from the slopes of an extinct volcano in Basilicata. The vines grow at 200 to 700 m on volcanic soil. It cannot be sold until the third year after harvest, and Riserva waits until the fifth.

claims.claim: Aglianico del Vulture was a DOC by DPR of 18 February 1971. The Superiore became a DOCG by ministerial decree of 2 August 2010 (Gazzetta Ufficiale 188, 13 August 2010).
The DOCG has two types: Aglianico del Vulture Superiore and Superiore Riserva.
The wine is made from Aglianico del Vulture (Aglianico) only.

The zone covers the whole territory of 15 communes in the province of Potenza, including Rionero in Vulture, Barile, Rapolla, Ripacandida, Ginestra, Maschito, Forenza, Acerenza, Melfi, Atella, Venosa, Lavello, Palazzo San Gervasio, Banzi and Genzano di Lucania. Three administrative islands of Atella are excluded.

The zone lies on the slopes of Monte Vulture, an extinct volcano that was active until the late Pleistocene. Its highest point is 1,327 m. Eruptions began about 800,000 years ago and left layers of lava and ash.
Vineyards must be on hills of mainly volcanic origin. Soils run from sandy and volcanic-ash sands to silty clay. Tuff layers act as a water store in the dry summer.
Vineyards must lie between 200 and 700 m above sea level.
The general exposure is east and south-east.
The climate is clearly dry in July and August. The volcanic massif brings breezes and ventilation from both coasts.
Vines are trained as alberello or simple trellis. New plantings must have at least 3,350 vines per hectare.
Grape yield is capped at 8 tonnes per hectare. Wine yield is capped at 65% of the grapes (52 hl/ha), with a tolerance up to 70%. Grapes must reach at least 13.0% natural alcohol.
Superiore cannot be sold before 1 November of the third year after the harvest. It needs at least 12 months in wood and at least 12 months in bottle.
Riserva needs release from 1 November of the fifth year after the harvest, with at least 24 months in wood and at least 12 months in bottle.
Finished wine needs at least 13.5% total alcohol (both Superiore and Riserva), 4.5 g/l total acidity and 26 g/l extract. The vintage must be on the label.
The disciplinare describes a deep ruby red turning garnet, with orange tints as it ages. It is dry, fairly tannic, savoury, persistent and balanced, and may show light wood notes.
The Superiore is said to be the only DOCG in Basilicata.
